Q115861632.summary: In the centre of this ivory triptych Christ rises in a mandorla carried by four angels, while beneath him the Virgin stands with raised arms among two groups of six disciples. On the wings, apostles stand beneath arches on twisted columns: on the right Peter and Andrew, recognisable by their attributes, and on the left probably Paul and Matthew. The choice of saints ties this vision of the ascended Lord to the cities of southern Italy where it was made.
facts: The Louvre suggests the saints were chosen for local reasons: Andrew is the patron of Amalfi and Matthew of Salerno.
The ivory was once inlaid with pearls.
It was given to the Louvre in 1909 by the Paris dealer Siegfried Ratzersdorfer.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: In a broad strip beneath the verses 'Be angry, and sin not … Offer the sacrifices of righteousness', the haloed Christ stands beside an altar with a chalice and stretches out his hand toward a group of men, one of whom turns away, while another figure approaches from the right.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-90-christ.summary: In the centre of the drawing the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding a book and a spear, stands in a mandorla supported by angels, treading on a lion and an adder and striking the adder's mouth with his spear: 'thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder'. The psalmist watches in astonishment from 'the secret place of the Most High'. The image belongs to the tradition of Christ the victor over evil seen in Carolingian ivories.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-90-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-anointing-in-h.summary: In a richly curtained hall Christ sits at a bench with Simon the Pharisee and his guests, holding a book and turning to address them, while the sinful woman crouches beneath him and anoints his feet. Christ's gesture defends her: 'her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much'.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
The Bayerische Staatsbibliothek has published the whole manuscript online with a Public Domain Mark, so every page can be studied in detail.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-anointing-in-h.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 318); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:monumental-sant-aquilino-christ-apos.summary: In the semi-dome of a niche, a young, beardless Christ with a halo bearing the Chi-Rho sits at the centre, raising his right hand as he speaks, while the twelve apostles sit around him in a semicircle against a gold ground; a box of scrolls stands at his feet. Like a classical philosopher among his pupils, Christ is shown as the true teacher. It is among the earliest surviving gold-ground mosaics of Christ.
facts: The octagonal chapel, which may originally have been built as an imperial mausoleum, adjoins the late-4th-century basilica of San Lorenzo.
Wikipedia notes that the scene has been read both as a 'Traditio Legis' (Christ the Lawgiver) and as Christ the Teacher among his apostles.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/3various/7byzanti.summary: In the golden semi-dome of the apse the Virgin, in a dark maphorion, sits on a jewelled throne with the Christ Child on her lap; he wears gold, has a cross-inscribed halo and raises his hand in blessing, while the hand of God above holds a wreath over them. Two archangels flank the throne, and beyond them stand saints and local clergy, among them Bishop Euphrasius holding a model of his church. A border of medallions of female martyrs centred on the Lamb of God frames the scene, which places the Mother of God and her Son in the position of heavenly majesty.
facts: Wikipedia describes this as the only surviving depiction of the Mother of God in the apse of an early Christian basilica in the West.
Among the figures is St Maurus, first bishop of Poreč, and a small child identified by inscription as Euphrasius, son of the archdeacon Claudius.
The Euphrasian Basilica has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1997.
wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/3various/7byzanti.notes: WGA dates the mosaic c. 540, but the present basilica was built from 553 under Bishop Euphrasius (construction took about ten years), so the apse mosaic is redated to the mid-6th century. Location spelling corrected from 'Poreè'.
